chapters.title: Haggai 1
body: The question lands bluntly: "is it time for you... to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" The people hadn't abandoned God outright — they'd just quietly prioritized their own comfortable homes over the unfinished temple, for long enough that it stopped feeling like a decision at all. Haggai's one job is simply naming what they'd stopped noticing.

What's easy to miss is how the people actually respond: not defensively, but by getting up and working. Whatever version of "the temple lying waste" you've quietly stopped noticing in your own life — something good left unfinished while comfort took priority — this chapter suggests the response doesn't have to be complicated. Just start.

chapters.title: Haggai 2
body: Some who remembered the first temple look at this smaller, humbler rebuilding and see it as "nothing" by comparison. God's answer isn't to dispute the comparison — it's to promise that "the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former," and "in this place will I give peace." Size and memory of better days aren't the measure here.

If something you're rebuilding right now feels embarrassingly small next to what it used to be, or what you hoped for, this chapter doesn't argue you out of noticing the difference. It just insists the difference isn't the final verdict on what this version can still become.
